subject: Mathematics
title: Asha's Market Adventure: Counting to 1000
hook: Help Asha organize the fruit stall and learn how to count and write big numbers!

characters.name: Asha
characters.role: curious girl helping at her parents' fruit stall

slides.title: Numbers up to 1000
slides.storyContext: Asha is helping at her family's fruit stall in the morning market.

image.alt: Numbers up to 1000 — Numbers up to 1000

slides.title: The Fruit Stall Mystery
slides.storyContext: Papa says, 'Asha, count all our mangoes today!' There are so many! Asha starts counting: 1, 2, 3... but she loses track after 50. Her friend Ravi says, 'Let's make groups!' When they count 100 mangoes, Papa brings another basket with 100, then another. Now there are 300 mangoes! But how do we write 300 properly?

image.alt: The Fruit Stall Mystery — Numbers up to 1000

slides.title: Why Counting Big Numbers is Hard
slides.storyContext: Asha tries counting mangoes one by one: '1, 2, 3...' She gets to 50 and loses track. 'I forget where I was!' Ravi laughs. 'That's why we make groups. It's faster and easier!'

slides.title: Hundreds, Tens, and Ones
slides.storyContext: Ravi teaches Asha: 'We can break big numbers into groups. 100 is called ONE HUNDRED. Look—one group of 100 mangoes.'

points.label: 100 (one hundred)
points.text: one full group of 10 tens

points.label: 10 (one ten)
points.text: one group of 10 ones

points.label: 1 (one)
points.text: the smallest unit

example.problem: If we have 3 groups of 100 mangoes, how many mangoes in total?

slides.inSimpleWords: A hundred is like 10 groups of 10. Three hundreds means 3 groups of 10 groups of 10.

slides.title: Breaking Down 300 Mangoes
slides.storyContext: Asha sees three big baskets of mangoes, each with 100. She writes on her clipboard: 100 + 100 + 100.

example.problem: How many mangoes in 3 baskets if each has 100?

slides.title: Adding More Mangoes to the Mix
slides.storyContext: Papa brings another batch! Now Asha has 300 mangoes from the three baskets, plus 5 more small groups of 10 mangoes (50 mangoes), plus 4 loose mangoes. 'Ravi, what's the total?' Ravi scratches his head and starts organizing.

slides.title: Writing Numbers: 347
slides.storyContext: Now Papa brings 3 more baskets of 100, and also 4 small groups of 10, and 7 loose mangoes. Asha writes the number carefully.

points.label: 3 Hundreds place
points.text: the number 3 in the 'hundreds' spot means 300

points.label: 4 Tens place
points.text: the number 4 in the 'tens' spot means 40

points.label: 7 Ones place
points.text: the number 7 in the 'ones' spot means 7

example.problem: Write: 300 + 40 + 7 as one number

slides.inSimpleWords: Each spot in a number tells you how many hundreds, tens, or ones there are. Left to right: biggest to smallest.

slides.title: Building 347 Step by Step
slides.storyContext: Asha lines up the mangoes: 3 big baskets (hundreds), 4 small bundles (tens), 7 single mangoes. She points to each group and says the number parts aloud.

example.problem: Show 347 as: ___ hundreds + ___ tens + ___ ones

slides.title: Expanded Form: What Every Digit Means
slides.storyContext: Ravi writes on the ground with chalk: 347 = 300 + 40 + 7. 'Each digit tells us a part of the whole number!'

points.label: Expanded form
points.text: breaks a number into its place-value parts

points.label: Each part has a name
points.text: hundreds, tens, ones

example.problem: Write 562 in expanded form

slides.inSimpleWords: Expanded form shows the value hiding inside each digit.

slides.title: Comparing Numbers: Which Stall Has More?
slides.storyContext: Next to Asha's stall is Meera's stall with 258 apples, and across is Vikram's stall with 385 apples. Who has more?

points.label: Compare hundreds first
points.text: 258 has 2 hundreds, 385 has 3 hundreds. 3 is bigger!

points.label: If hundreds are equal, compare tens
points.text: Look at the middle digit

points.label: If tens are equal, compare ones
points.text: Look at the last digit

example.problem: Compare 258 and 385. Which is bigger?
example.solution: 385 > 258 because 3 hundreds > 2 hundreds. Vikram's stall has more apples.

slides.inSimpleWords: To compare big numbers, look at the hundreds place first. The one with more hundreds is always bigger.

slides.title: Comparing Three Stalls
slides.storyContext: Asha now knows three fruit sellers: Meera (258), Vikram (385), and Suresh (312). She wants to order them by who has most fruit.

example.problem: Order 258, 385, and 312 from biggest to smallest

slides.title: Ordering on the Number Line
slides.storyContext: Asha draws a number line to show all the stalls' fruit counts from smallest to biggest: 100, 200, 300, 400, 500...

points.label: Each number is 100 more
points.text: 400 is 100 more than 300

points.label: 1000 is the biggest!
points.text: one thousand = 10 groups of 100

slides.inSimpleWords: Skip counting by 100s helps us see patterns and order numbers quickly.

slides.title: Ravi's Skip-Counting Song
slides.storyContext: Ravi teaches Asha a rhythm: 'One hundred, two hundred, three hundred...' They clap as they count by 100s all the way to 1000. Papa laughs and joins in!

slides.title: Grouping by 10s and 1s
slides.storyContext: Asha now counts the oranges: she has 412 oranges. She counts: 1 group of 100, then 1 group of 100, then 1 group of 100, then 1 group of 100. Now 4 groups of 10 (that's 40). And 2 loose oranges.

points.label: 412 = 4 hundreds + 1 ten + 2 ones
points.text: 4 groups of 100 + 1 group of 10 + 2 loose

example.problem: Break 573 into hundreds, tens, and ones

slides.inSimpleWords: Every number up to 1000 is just groups of 100, plus groups of 10, plus leftover ones.

slides.title: Decomposing 789
slides.storyContext: Papa has 789 bananas to sell. Asha breaks it down using baskets and loose bananas: 7 baskets of 100, 8 bundles of 10, and 9 single bananas.

example.problem: Write 789 as: ___ hundreds + ___ tens + ___ ones

slides.title: Representing Numbers on a Thousands Frame
slides.storyContext: Ravi shows Asha a chart with boxes: 10 rows of 10 columns (100 squares per row, 1000 total). He shades some squares and says, 'This shows 347 out of 1000!'

points.label: A thousands frame has 1000 squares
points.text: 10 rows × 10 columns × 10 layers = 1000

points.label: Each row is 100 squares
points.text: Shade 3-and-a-half rows to show 347

points.label: See place value visually
points.text: Helps you understand what 347 looks like out of 1000

example.problem: Show 500 on a thousands frame. How many rows?
example.solution: 5 rows of 100 squares each = 500 squares shaded

slides.inSimpleWords: A thousands frame is like a visual map of numbers from 1 to 1000.

slides.title: The Big Count Challenge
slides.storyContext: At day's end, Asha counts the total sales. Papa sold 623 mangoes, Ravi helped count 178 bananas from another section. Asha wants to know: is 623 bigger than 178? Can she write 623 in words?

example.problem: Write 623 in words and tell: is 623 > 178? Why?
example.solution: 623 is 'six hundred twenty-three.' Yes, 623 > 178 because 6 hundreds > 1 hundred.

slides.title: Asha Counts Her Way to Success
slides.storyContext: By the end of the day, Asha has used numbers from 1 to 1000 many times! She confidently announces the totals to Papa, who is proud. 'My daughter is a mathematician!' he cheers.

slides.title: Reading and Writing Numbers in Words
slides.storyContext: Asha's friend Mali asks, 'How do you say 456?' Asha says carefully: 'Four hundred fifty-six.' Ravi writes it down: F-O-U-R H-U-N-D-R-E-D F-I-F-T-Y-S-I-X.

points.label: Say hundreds first
points.text: 456 → 'four hundred'

points.label: Then the tens and ones
points.text: 'fifty-six' (not 'fifty and six')

points.label: Practice: 789
points.text: 'seven hundred eighty-nine'

example.problem: Write these in words: 234, 501, 999
example.solution: Two hundred thirty-four, Five hundred one, Nine hundred ninety-nine

slides.inSimpleWords: Say the hundreds part, then the tens-and-ones part. Use a hyphen for twenty-one through ninety-nine.

slides.title: Number Ordering Challenge
slides.storyContext: Asha's cousin Priya brings four cards with numbers: 678, 543, 789, 601. Asha arranges them from smallest to largest using what she learned.

example.problem: Order 678, 543, 789, 601 from smallest to largest

slides.title: Even and Odd Numbers
slides.storyContext: Ravi notices something: 'When I count mangoes in pairs (2, 2, 2...), some numbers run out perfectly, and some have 1 left over!' Asha learns: even numbers divide evenly, odd numbers have 1 left.

points.label: Even numbers
points.text: Can be split into 2 equal groups: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10...

points.label: Odd numbers
points.text: Always have 1 left over: 1, 3, 5, 7, 9...

points.label: Look at the ones digit
points.text: Even ends in 0, 2, 4, 6, 8. Odd ends in 1, 3, 5, 7, 9

example.problem: Is 347 even or odd? Is 500 even or odd?
example.solution: 347 is odd (ends in 7). 500 is even (ends in 0).

slides.inSimpleWords: Check the last digit: even ends in 0, 2, 4, 6, 8.

slides.title: Identifying Even and Odd from a Basket
slides.storyContext: Asha counts: 'Papa has 236 mangoes—that's even (ends in 6). Ravi has 145 bananas—that's odd (ends in 5).'

example.problem: List three even numbers between 100 and 1000
example.solution: Any three ending in 0, 2, 4, 6, or 8. Example: 234, 567 is odd, 890 is even

slides.title: Your Turn: Sort the Inventory
slides.storyContext: Here are the counts from four fruit sellers on the same street: Stall A: 451 grapes, Stall B: 348 grapes, Stall C: 520 grapes, Stall D: 275 grapes. Arrange them from smallest to biggest!

example.problem: Order these: 451, 348, 520, 275 from smallest to biggest

slides.title: Challenge: Build Numbers from Digits
slides.storyContext: Asha has digit cards: 3, 5, 7. She wants to build the biggest number possible using all three. Ravi says, 'Put them in order from biggest to smallest!'

example.problem: Use digits 3, 5, 7 to make the biggest and smallest 3-digit numbers

slides.title: Place Value in Action: 200 vs. 20 vs. 2
slides.storyContext: Asha realizes something amazing: the digit 2 can mean 2, or 20, or 200—depending on where it sits! She shows Ravi three numbers: 200, 20, 2.

points.label: 2 in the ones place
points.text: means just 2

points.label: 2 in the tens place
points.text: means 20 (ten times bigger!)

points.label: 2 in the hundreds place
points.text: means 200 (one hundred times bigger!)

example.problem: What does the 5 mean in each number: 5, 50, 500?

slides.inSimpleWords: The position of a digit determines its true value.

slides.title: Decomposing Real Numbers from the Market
slides.storyContext: Papa brings a ledger showing daily sales: Tuesday 456 items, Wednesday 823 items, Thursday 539 items. Asha breaks each into place values for easy reading.

example.problem: Show 456, 823, 539 in expanded form

points.text: Numbers up to 1000 are made of hundreds, tens, and ones
Compare by looking at hundreds first, then tens, then ones
We can write numbers in expanded form (e.g., 347 = 300 + 40 + 7)
Skip counting by 100s helps us see patterns: 100, 200, 300...
Place value: the position of a digit determines its meaning
Every number can be read in words and written in standard form
Even numbers end in 0, 2, 4, 6, 8; odd numbers end in 1, 3, 5, 7, 9

subject: Mathematics
title: Ravi's Cricket Tournament: Adding and Subtracting
hook: Ravi is organizing a cricket tournament. Learn addition and subtraction as he keeps score and counts players!

characters.name: Neha
characters.role: Ravi's friend who helps with scorekeeping

slides.title: Addition and Subtraction
slides.storyContext: Ravi is excited! His school is hosting a cricket tournament, and he's keeping the score.

image.alt: Addition and Subtraction — Addition and Subtraction

slides.title: Keeping Cricket Scores
slides.storyContext: On Day 1, Team Red scores 156 runs in the first innings. Coach Aman asks Ravi: 'If Team Blue scores 243 runs, do they win or lose?' Ravi scratches his head. 'I need to add and subtract big numbers!' Neha says, 'Let's line them up properly and use place values!'

slides.title: Why Ravi Needs Addition and Subtraction
slides.storyContext: Ravi realizes his job is tricky. He must add up runs across multiple innings and subtract penalties. 'This is real mathematics!' Coach Aman nods.

slides.title: Adding 1-Digit Numbers: The Basics
slides.storyContext: Ravi starts simple. First practice session: Team A gets 5 runs, then 3 more runs. Neha asks, 'How many total?'

points.text: Count on from 5: 6, 7, 8. Answer: 8

points.label: Use your fingers or objects
points.text: 5 fingers, add 3 more fingers

points.label: Say it aloud
points.text: 'Five plus three equals eight'

example.problem: A batter hits 7 runs. The next batter hits 4. Total?

slides.inSimpleWords: Adding means putting groups together. Count on to find the answer.

slides.title: Quick Addition Practice
slides.storyContext: Ravi practices: 6 + 2 = ? He counts on: 7, 8. Answer: 8. He's getting faster!

example.problem: Add these pairs: 3 + 4, 5 + 5, 2 + 7

slides.title: Subtracting 1-Digit Numbers: The Basics
slides.storyContext: Team Green had 9 runs but loses 4 runs due to a penalty. Ravi counts back on his fingers: 9, 8, 7, 6, 5. 'That's 5 left!'

points.text: Count back from 9: 8, 7, 6, 5. Answer: 5

points.label: Subtraction means taking away
points.text: Start at the bigger number, count back

points.label: Say it aloud
points.text: 'Nine minus four equals five'

example.problem: Team had 12 runs, lost 5. How many left?

slides.inSimpleWords: Subtraction means taking away. Count back to find the answer.

slides.title: Adding 2-Digit Numbers: Ones First
slides.storyContext: First practice: Team A has 24 players, Team B brings 13 players. How many total? Ravi writes them in columns.

points.label: Line up ones and tens
points.text: 24 means 2 tens + 4 ones; 13 means 1 ten + 3 ones

points.label: Add the ones first
points.text: 4 + 3 = 7 ones

points.label: Add the tens next
points.text: 2 + 1 = 3 tens

points.label: Read the answer
points.text: 3 tens + 7 ones = 37

slides.inSimpleWords: Line up the numbers by place value, add ones first, then tens.

slides.title: Adding More 2-Digit Numbers
slides.storyContext: Practice match scores: Team A scores 32 runs, Team B scores 45 runs. Ravi wants to know the combined total of both teams.

slides.title: Subtracting 2-Digit Numbers: No Borrowing
slides.storyContext: Neha says, 'Team Green had 48 runs but lost 13 runs because of a penalty. How many are left?'

points.label: Line up by place value
points.text: Write 48 on top, 13 below

points.label: Subtract ones first
points.text: 8 - 3 = 5 ones

points.label: Subtract tens next
points.text: 4 - 1 = 3 tens

points.label: Answer: 35
points.text: 48 - 13 = 35 runs left

slides.inSimpleWords: Subtraction is taking away. Line up the numbers and subtract ones first, then tens.

slides.title: Subtracting More 2-Digit Numbers
slides.storyContext: Team Yellow had 67 runs from the first innings. In the second innings, they lost 24 runs due to mistakes. Ravi calculates.

slides.title: Adding 3-Digit Numbers: Carrying Over
slides.storyContext: Now the real challenge! Team Red scored 156 runs in one match, Team Red scores 245 runs in another match. What's the total?

points.label: Add the ones: 6 + 5 = 11
points.text: 11 = 1 ten and 1 one. Write 1, carry 1 ten

points.label: Add the tens: 1 (carried) + 5 + 4 = 10
points.text: 10 tens = 1 hundred and 0 tens. Write 0, carry 1 hundred

points.label: Add the hundreds: 1 (carried) + 1 + 2 = 4
points.text: Write 4 hundreds

slides.inSimpleWords: When ones add up to 10 or more, that's a new ten! Move it to the tens place.

slides.title: Carrying Over in Action
slides.storyContext: Ravi practices more: 328 + 164. He carefully carries as ones and tens overflow into the next place value.

slides.title: Subtracting with Borrowing
slides.storyContext: Coach Aman asks: 'Team Blue had 332 runs. They lost 147 runs in a mistake. How many left?'

points.label: Look at ones: 2 - 7. Can't do it!
points.text: Borrow 1 ten from the tens place

points.label: Now ones: 12 - 7 = 5 ones
points.text: We turned 1 ten into 10 ones

points.label: Tens: 2 tens (left after borrowing) - 4 tens. Can't do it!
points.text: Borrow 1 hundred

points.label: Now tens: 12 - 4 = 8 tens
points.text: And hundreds: 2 - 1 = 1

slides.inSimpleWords: When you can't subtract, borrow from the next place value (like borrowing money from a friend!)

slides.title: Borrowing in Action
slides.storyContext: Ravi practices: 423 - 156. His ones digit is too small, so he borrows. He gets 267 as the answer.

example.solution: Ones: can't do 3 - 6, borrow → 13 - 6 = 7. Tens: can't do 1 - 5, borrow → 11 - 5 = 6. Hundreds: 3 - 1 = 2. Answer: 267

slides.title: Word Problems: Adding Runs Across Innings
slides.storyContext: Team Yellow scored 123 runs in the first innings, 156 runs in the second, and 87 runs in the third. Total?

points.label: Check your work
points.text: Does 366 make sense?

slides.inSimpleWords: To add more than two numbers, add the first two, then add the third to that answer.

slides.title: Tournament Final Score
slides.storyContext: Final match! Team Red (467 runs) vs Team Blue (389 runs). By how many runs does Red win?

example.problem: Find the difference: 467 - 389

slides.title: Ravi Becomes the Tournament Hero
slides.storyContext: By tournament's end, Ravi has added and subtracted hundreds of scores. Coach Aman hugs him: 'You kept perfect records! This is real mathematics in action!'

slides.title: Fact Families: Related Addition and Subtraction
slides.storyContext: Neha discovers something cool: if 3 + 5 = 8, then 5 + 3 = 8, and 8 - 3 = 5, and 8 - 5 = 3. They all connect!

points.label: Addition is commutative
points.text: 3 + 5 = 8 and 5 + 3 = 8 (same answer!)

points.label: Subtraction undoes addition
points.text: 8 - 3 = 5 is the 'opposite' of 3 + 5 = 8

example.problem: Write all fact families for 4, 6, and 10

slides.inSimpleWords: Addition and subtraction are opposites. They always come in related groups.

slides.title: Using Fact Families to Check Answers
slides.storyContext: Ravi adds 47 + 23 = 70. To check, he subtracts: 70 - 23 should equal 47. It does! He's confident in his answer.

example.problem: Check: 156 + 245 = 401 using subtraction

slides.title: Missing Number Problems
slides.storyContext: Coach asks Ravi: 'Team A scored some runs, Team B scored 34 more, and together they scored 127. How many did Team A score?'

example.problem: What number plus 45 equals 120?

slides.inSimpleWords: Work backwards using subtraction to find missing numbers.

slides.title: Your Turn: Cricket Tournament Math
slides.storyContext: Three teams' scores: Team A: 234 runs, Team B: 156 runs, Team C: 289 runs. (a) How many more runs does C have than B? (b) What's the total of all three teams?

example.solution: (a) 289 - 156 = 133 runs more for C. (b) 234 + 156 + 289 = 679 runs total

slides.title: Challenge: Complex Tournament Scenarios
slides.storyContext: Team Red scored 345 runs in Match 1 and 267 runs in Match 2. Team Blue scored 412 runs in Match 1 and 298 runs in Match 2. Which team scored more total? By how much?

example.problem: Red total: 345 + 267. Blue total: 412 + 298. Find the difference.

slides.title: Ravi's Scorecard Blues
slides.storyContext: Day 2: Ravi adds 234 + 156 + 189 (scores across three matches). He realizes: 'This is getting complex! I need a system.'

slides.title: Grouping Numbers for Easier Calculation
slides.storyContext: Coach Aman shows Ravi: 'Instead of adding 3 big numbers at once, add the first two, then add the third to the result.'

example.problem: Add 112 + 225 + 143 step-by-step

slides.inSimpleWords: Break big addition into smaller chunks. Add two, then add the third.

slides.title: Verifying Tournament Results
slides.storyContext: Ravi checks: Team A (123 + 167 + 145). He calculates step by step and double-checks using fact families.

slides.title: Zero in Addition and Subtraction
slides.storyContext: Neha asks: 'What if a team scores 0 runs in an innings?' Ravi learns: 'Zero means nothing was added. The total stays the same.'

points.label: Adding zero
points.text: 52 + 0 = 52 (adding nothing changes nothing)

points.label: Subtracting zero
points.text: 52 - 0 = 52 (taking away nothing leaves everything)

points.label: Zero as the first number
points.text: 0 + 45 = 45 (starting from nothing, then adding 45)

slides.inSimpleWords: Zero doesn't change the answer. Adding or subtracting zero keeps the number the same.

points.text: Always line up numbers by place value (ones under ones, tens under tens)
For addition: add ones first, then tens, then hundreds
When ones add to 10+, carry a ten to the tens place
For subtraction: subtract ones first, then tens, then hundreds
If you can't subtract, borrow from the next place value
Word problems: read carefully, decide if you add or subtract, then solve
Addition and subtraction are opposites (fact families)
Use subtraction to check your addition, and vice versa

subject: Mathematics
title: Priya's Garden Project: Learning Measurement
hook: Priya is growing a garden at home. Learn how to measure length, weight, and capacity!

characters.name: Grandma
characters.role: wise grandmother who teaches traditional measures

characters.name: Arjun
characters.role: Priya's cousin who helps with the garden

slides.title: Measurement
slides.storyContext: Priya starts a vegetable garden in her backyard. She needs to measure everything!

slides.title: Growing a Garden
slides.storyContext: Grandma says, 'Priya, to grow sunflowers, you need to know how tall they'll get. And tomatoes need a pot that holds enough water.' Arjun asks, 'How do we measure?' Grandma brings out a ruler, a weighing scale, and a water jug. 'These are our tools!'

slides.title: Why Measurement Matters in Gardening
slides.storyContext: Priya realizes: 'If I don't know the height of the garden fence, I can't plant tall sunflowers there. If I don't track the water, my plants die!' Measurement is essential.

slides.title: What is Measurement?
slides.storyContext: Priya wonders: 'How do we know if something is big or small, heavy or light, full or empty?' Grandma explains: 'We use measurement to compare things.'

points.label: Measurement compares
points.text: Measures show how much of something we have

points.label: We measure three things
points.text: Length (how long), Weight (how heavy), Capacity (how much liquid)

points.label: We use tools and units
points.text: Rulers, scales, and jugs measure in centimeters, grams, and liters

example.problem: What do we measure to find: (a) if a stick is long? (b) if a bag is heavy? (c) if a bottle is full?

slides.inSimpleWords: Measurement tells us how big, how heavy, or how full something is.

slides.title: Measuring Length: Centimeters and Meters
slides.storyContext: Priya's sunflower seedling is tiny. 'How tall is it?' She uses a ruler marked in centimeters (cm).

points.label: Centimeter (cm)
points.text: a small unit. A fingernail is about 1 cm wide

points.label: Meter (m)
points.text: a bigger unit. 100 cm = 1 meter (about the height of a door)

points.label: Measure carefully
points.text: Line the ruler at the zero mark and read where it ends

example.problem: Priya's seedling is 12 cm tall today. In 2 weeks, it's 34 cm. How much did it grow?

slides.inSimpleWords: Centimeters measure small things (fingers, seeds), meters measure bigger things (doors, gardens).

slides.title: Measuring Garden Plants
slides.storyContext: Priya measures her growing plants weekly: Week 1 tomato is 8 cm, Week 2 it's 15 cm, Week 3 it's 23 cm. She tracks the changes.

example.problem: How much did the tomato grow from Week 1 to Week 3?

slides.title: Comparing Lengths
slides.storyContext: Arjun grows carrots. His longest carrot is 18 cm. Priya's longest is 15 cm. 'Who grew the longer carrot?'

points.label: Compare two lengths
points.text: 18 cm > 15 cm. Arjun's is longer

points.label: The difference
points.text: 18 - 15 = 3 cm longer

points.label: Order from shortest to longest
points.text: Use comparison symbols: <, >, =

example.problem: Arjun's carrot: 18 cm, Priya's: 15 cm. Order from shortest to longest.

slides.inSimpleWords: Compare by measuring both and seeing which number is bigger.

slides.title: Measuring Weight: Kilograms and Grams
slides.storyContext: Priya picks her first tomato! 'How heavy is it?' Grandma puts it on a weighing scale.

points.label: Gram (g)
points.text: a tiny unit. A paperclip weighs about 1 gram

points.label: Kilogram (kg)
points.text: a heavy unit. 1000 grams = 1 kilogram (like a big bag of rice)

points.label: Scale shows weight
points.text: Read the number where the needle stops

example.problem: One tomato weighs 120 grams. Priya picks 5 tomatoes of the same weight. Total weight?

slides.inSimpleWords: Grams measure light things, kilograms measure heavy things like food at the market.

slides.title: Weighing Garden Produce
slides.storyContext: Priya harvests vegetables: tomato 150 g, carrot 120 g, eggplant 180 g. She weighs each and records the amounts.

example.problem: Total weight of all three vegetables?

slides.title: Measuring Capacity: Liters and Milliliters
slides.storyContext: Every morning, Priya waters her plants. Grandma gives her a water jug. 'This jug holds 1 liter. How much water does the garden need?'

points.label: Milliliter (mL)
points.text: a small amount. A teaspoon holds about 5 mL

points.label: Liter (L)
points.text: a bigger amount. 1000 mL = 1 liter (like a water bottle)

points.label: Measure with a jug
points.text: Pour carefully and read the markings on the side

example.problem: Priya waters 8 plants, using 2 liters per plant. How much water total?

slides.inSimpleWords: Milliliters are for tiny amounts (medicine, juice), liters are for bigger amounts (water, milk).

slides.title: Watering the Garden
slides.storyContext: Priya's garden has 5 tomato pots, 3 carrot pots, and 2 herb pots. Each pot needs 1 liter of water. How much water in total?

example.problem: Total pots: 5 + 3 + 2 = 10 pots. Water needed?
example.solution: 10 pots × 1 liter = 10 liters of water total

slides.title: Comparing and Adding Measurements
slides.storyContext: Arjun grows carrots. His longest carrot is 18 cm. Priya's longest is 15 cm. 'Let's put them together in a line!'

points.label: Compare two measurements
points.text: 18 cm > 15 cm. Arjun's is longer

points.label: Add measurements
points.text: 18 + 15 = 33 cm if lined end-to-end

points.label: Subtract measurements
points.text: 18 - 15 = 3 cm. Arjun's is 3 cm longer

example.problem: Add these lengths: 25 cm + 34 cm + 18 cm = ?

slides.inSimpleWords: You can add and subtract measurements just like regular numbers!

slides.title: Time and Growth: Days and Weeks
slides.storyContext: Priya keeps a garden diary. 'My tomato plant was 10 cm on Day 1. Now it's Day 21, and it's 45 cm. How much grew each week?'

points.label: Measure growth over time
points.text: Record height on Day 1, Day 8, Day 15, Day 22

points.label: Calculate week-by-week growth
points.text: Subtract to find the difference

points.label: Compare weeks
points.text: Which week had the most growth?

example.problem: Day 1: 10 cm, Day 8: 18 cm, Day 15: 32 cm, Day 22: 45 cm. Growth in Week 2?

slides.inSimpleWords: Measure over time to see how fast plants grow. Subtraction shows you the change!

slides.title: Tracking Plant Growth Chart
slides.storyContext: Priya creates a chart of her sunflower's height: Week 1: 5 cm, Week 2: 12 cm, Week 3: 22 cm, Week 4: 35 cm. She notices it grows faster each week!

example.problem: Which week had the most growth? Week 1→2, 2→3, or 3→4?
example.solution: Week 1→2: 7 cm. Week 2→3: 10 cm. Week 3→4: 13 cm. Week 3→4 had most growth!

slides.title: Converting Between Units
slides.storyContext: Grandma says: 'If your plant is 100 cm tall, that's 1 meter. If you harvest 2 kilograms of tomatoes, that's 2000 grams!'

points.label: 100 centimeters = 1 meter
points.text: Bigger unit, fewer of them needed

points.label: 1000 grams = 1 kilogram
points.text: Smaller units make bigger measurements

example.problem: Priya's carrot is 20 cm. How much shorter than 1 meter?
example.solution: 1 meter = 100 cm. 100 - 20 = 80 cm shorter than 1 meter

slides.inSimpleWords: Big units and small units measure the same thing differently.

slides.title: Converting Real Garden Measurements
slides.storyContext: Priya measures her sunflower: 156 cm tall. 'Is that more than 1 meter?' She calculates: 156 cm = 1 meter 56 cm, or 1.56 meters.

example.problem: Convert: 156 cm = ? meters and ? cm

slides.title: The Garden Harvest Report
slides.storyContext: End of the season! Priya reports: Sunflower height: 187 cm. Tomatoes harvested: 12 kg total. Water used: 240 liters. What was her biggest plant?

example.problem: Compare plant height: Sunflower 187 cm vs. Grandma's record sunflower 156 cm. How much taller?
example.solution: 187 - 156 = 31 cm. Priya's sunflower is 31 cm taller!

slides.title: Priya Wins the Garden Contest
slides.storyContext: The school's 'Best Garden' competition measures all student gardens by height of tallest plant, total harvest weight, and efficiency of water use. Priya's measurements show her garden is a winner!

slides.title: Estimating Measurements
slides.storyContext: Arjun looks at a plant and guesses: 'This is about 15 cm tall.' Then he measures: 14 cm. 'My estimate was close!' Grandma says: 'Estimation helps us know if our real measurement makes sense.'

points.label: Estimate first
points.text: Make a reasonable guess using what you know

points.label: Then measure
points.text: Use a ruler, scale, or jug to get the exact number

points.label: Compare
points.text: Is your estimate close to the real number?

example.problem: Estimate: Is a tomato heavier than 100 grams? Then weigh it.
example.solution: Estimate: yes, probably. Real: 120 grams. Estimate was close!

slides.inSimpleWords: Good estimators are ready for the real measurement.

slides.title: Practice Estimation in the Garden
slides.storyContext: Priya guesses: 'That watermelon looks like 3 kg.' She weighs it: 2.8 kg. 'Very close!'

example.problem: Estimate the height of a tomato plant, then measure
example.solution: Estimate: 30 cm. Actual: 32 cm. Good estimate!

slides.title: Your Turn: Measure Your Garden
slides.storyContext: You have three plants: Plant A is 24 cm tall and weighs 150 grams. Plant B is 35 cm tall and weighs 280 grams. Plant C is 18 cm tall and weighs 95 grams. (a) Which plant is tallest? (b) What's the total height? (c) Which plant weighs the most?

example.problem: (a) Compare heights: 24, 35, 18. (b) Add all heights. (c) Compare weights: 150, 280, 95.
example.solution: (a) Plant B at 35 cm. (b) 24 + 35 + 18 = 77 cm total. (c) Plant B at 280 grams

slides.title: Challenge: Multi-Step Measurement Problems
slides.storyContext: Priya's garden uses 20 liters of water per day for 7 days. Her plants gain a total of 5 kg of weight from all the growth. How much water used? How many grams of growth?

example.problem: (a) 20 liters × 7 days = ? (b) 5 kg = ? grams
example.solution: (a) 140 liters of water. (b) 5 × 1000 = 5000 grams of growth

slides.title: Comparing Measurements Across Units
slides.storyContext: Arjun says: 'My plant is 1 meter 20 centimeters. Priya's is 95 centimeters. Whose is taller?' Priya converts to compare.

points.label: Compare
points.text: 120 cm > 95 cm

example.problem: Compare: 1 meter 50 cm vs 145 cm

slides.inSimpleWords: Convert big units to small units, then compare the numbers.

slides.title: Real-World Unit Conversion: Harvest Day
slides.storyContext: Priya harvested 2 kg of tomatoes, 800 g of carrots, and 1 kg 200 g of peppers. She wants the total in kilograms.

example.problem: Convert and add: 2 kg + 800 g + (1 kg 200 g)

slides.title: Practical Measurement: Planting Spacing
slides.storyContext: Grandma teaches: 'Tomato plants need 30 cm between them. If you have 4 plants in a row, how much space total?'

points.label: Distance between plants
points.text: 30 cm is the standard spacing

points.label: Calculate total spacing
points.text: 4 plants need 3 gaps: 3 × 30 = 90 cm

points.label: Add extra for edges
points.text: Plus space at the start and end

example.problem: 5 plants with 25 cm spacing between them. Space needed?

slides.inSimpleWords: Real gardening uses measurement for layout and spacing.

points.text: Length is measured in centimeters (cm) and meters (m). 100 cm = 1 meter
Weight is measured in grams (g) and kilograms (kg). 1000 g = 1 kg
Capacity (how much liquid) is measured in milliliters (mL) and liters (L). 1000 mL = 1 L
You can add and subtract measurements like regular numbers
Measure the same thing over time to see how it changes
Different tools: ruler for length, scale for weight, jug for capacity
Estimate before measuring to check if your answer makes sense
Big units (m, kg, L) and small units (cm, g, mL) measure the same things differently
